scenario: AITA for telling an intern to throw her banana peel in the trash? | A few details to set the stage: To get into my place of work, one needs to walk from the parking lot down a sidewalk that is along the side of the building. The other side of the sidewalk is semi-wooded with low growing evergreen shrubs. This sidewalk is about 100ft long, and has a trash can at either end. Also, in the last month, there have been a ton of flies buzzing around this area, so much so that the building manager called an exterminator. This morning, I (\~30s F) witnessed an intern (20s F) for one of the companies in our building walking into work eating a banana. About 3/4 of the way down the sidewalk, with a trashcan not even 25 feet away, she tossed the banana peel into the bushes. It landed on top of the bush and she just kept walking. I wasn't sufficiently caffeinated to be polite, so I blurted out "What the hell? There's a trash can right in front of you!" complete with the WTF hand gesture; pointing to the trash can. I pointed at the peel sitting on top of the bush and told her to "pick up your (her) damn banana peel." Instead she cried loudly saying something unintelligible, got her peel, and put it in the trash. I'm thinking, great, this is over. Maybe she won't toss her banana debris into the bushes and we will have less flies. I'm sure I could have been more nice about it / sworn less, but I was just so shocked to see someone litter like that. I badged in to the building and she walked in behind me. At some point, she must have cried to her boss about it, because her boss found me today and asked if I confronted her intern. I said I had, then explained, as I have done here, about the banana peel. I guess she spent all morning crying about how "mean" I was and couldn't do any work. My brain was screaming "drama queen" but I apologized instead for upsetting the intern. We laughed together about absurdity of it all, especially over a banana peel! But now that it's the weekend and I'm sufficiently caffeinated, I'm wondering AITA for calling her out?

Wearing a suit and tie makes me feel confident. What do you think?

It’s great that wearing a suit and tie makes you feel confident—that’s a powerful connection between appearance and self-perception! Many people experience the same boost in confidence when dressing formally, and there’s actually some science behind it.

### Why It Works:
1. **Power Posing & Nonverbal Cues** – Studies (like Amy Cuddy’s research on "power posing") suggest that wearing formal attire can subtly influence how others perceive you, which in turn can make *you* feel more authoritative or capable. Even if it’s just psychological, the effect can be real.
2. **Ritual & Routine** – Dressing up can act as a mental cue, signaling to your brain that you’re entering a "high-stakes" or "professional" mode, which can sharpen focus and reduce anxiety.
3. **Social Norms** – In many professional settings, suits and ties are associated with competence, respect, and seriousness. When you align with those expectations, it can reinforce your own belief in your ability to succeed.
4. **Body Language Feedback** – Standing taller, holding your head high, and moving with purpose (often unconsciously when dressed formally) can amplify feelings of confidence.

### Potential Caveats:
- **Comfort Matters** – If the suit feels restrictive or uncomfortable, it might undermine confidence instead. Find a fit that’s both polished and *you*.
- **Context Matters** – In creative or casual environments, formal wear might feel out of place. Confidence isn’t tied to one style—it’s about authenticity.
- **Self-Fulfilling Prophecy** – If you *believe* the suit makes you confident, it likely will—even if others don’t notice. That’s the power of mindset!

### Pro Tip:
Pair the suit with a **posture check** (shoulders back, chin up) and **mindset reinforcement** (e.g., "I own this space"). The combo can create a compound effect.

Would you say the confidence boost is more about *how you feel* or *how others perceive you*? Or is it a mix?
